topic: The Global Migration of the Arctic Tern

text.content: By undertaking an annual journey that frequently exceeds 70,000 kilometers between northern breeding grounds and the Antarctic pack ice, a particular species of seabird experiences more annual daylight than any other organism on Earth. Known to researchers as the Arctic Tern, this small bird completes a massive trans-hemispheric migration every year.

Sustaining such an arduous flight relies on distinct anatomical adaptations. Having a minimal body mass significantly reduces the energy expenditure required for prolonged active flight. Furthermore, rather than maintaining continuous wing movement, efficient aerodynamic gliding over vast oceanic expanses is facilitated by long, narrow wings adapted to harness prevailing wind currents.

Navigating across featureless oceanic regions where visual landmarks such as coastal topography are absent presents a major physiological challenge. It is hypothesised by marine biologists that an internal biological mechanism directs this movement. Through the detection of geomagnetic field variations, accurate navigation over open water is achieved without reliance on terrestrial reference points.

Instead of following a direct latitudinal trajectory, the transit route exhibits significant curvature, aligned primarily with major marine currents rich in prey. Foraging during flight, these birds submerge to capture small fish and consume substantial quantities of marine crustaceans commonly referred to as krill.

Recent environmental changes pose a severe threat to this established migratory corridor. Driven by increases in sea surface temperatures, key prey distributions—including cold-water fish species and krill populations—are shifting geographically. Consequently, extended flight deviations from traditional routes are increasingly necessary for energetic maintenance, jeopardising the long-term viability of the migration.
